`rc`: start, stop and enable services.

## Synopsis

<strong>rc</strong>\
<strong>rc</strong> <em>name</em> <strong>start</strong>\|<strong>stop</strong>\|<strong>restart</strong>\|<strong>status</strong>\|<strong>enable</strong>\|<strong>disable</strong>\
<strong>rc</strong> <em>name action</em>\
<strong>rc boot</strong>

## Description

A service is a program that runs in the background (a daemon), started at boot or by hand. Each is a Lua script in <strong>/etc/rc.d</strong>, named for it, run in an environment of its own where <strong>name</strong> is its name. It sets, as OpenRC's scripts do:

<strong>command</strong>
: The program, as a path.

<strong>command\_args</strong>
: Its arguments: a list, or a string split on spaces.

<strong>description</strong>
: What it is.

<strong>output\_log</strong>
: A file its output and errors are added to; <strong>/dev/null</strong> when not given.

From those, <strong>rc</strong> gives it the actions below. A function the script defines by one of their names (start, stop, status) is used instead, and any other function it defines is an action too: <strong>rc</strong> <em>name action</em> calls it (its return value, a number, is the exit status). For example:

```text
description = "remote shell daemon"
command = "/bin/mcsshd"
command_args = {"-p", "22"}
function reload()
  require("sys").kill(tonumber(io.open("/run/" .. name .. ".pid"):read("l")), "SIGHUP")
end
```

With no arguments, <strong>rc</strong> lists the services: each one's name, whether it's enabled, and whether it's running.

## Actions

<strong>start</strong>
: Runs it in a session of its own, with no terminal (so no ^C at a terminal reaches it) and its input from <strong>/dev/null</strong>, and keeps its process id in <strong>/run/</strong><em>name</em><strong>.pid</strong><em>.</em>

<strong>stop</strong>
: Sends it SIGTERM, and SIGKILL if it hasn't ended within 5 seconds.

<strong>restart</strong>
: Stops it, then starts it.

<strong>status</strong>
: Says whether it's running.

<strong>enable</strong>, <strong>disable</strong>
: Sets <em>name</em><strong>\_enable=YES</strong> (or NO) in <strong>/etc/rc.conf</strong>: whether it starts at boot.

<strong>boot</strong>
: Starts every service enabled in <strong>/etc/rc.conf</strong>, in its order. <strong>/etc/rc</strong> runs it at boot: the kernel runs that script with <strong>sh</strong> before the console's shell starts (the <strong>rc=</strong> boot option names another).

## Exit status

0 on success; <strong>status</strong> 3 when it isn't running; 1 for a bad argument, a service that doesn't exist, or one that can't be started.

## Files

<strong>/etc/rc</strong>
: The boot's script.

<strong>/etc/rc.conf</strong>
: Which services start at boot.

<strong>/etc/rc.d/</strong><em>name</em>
: A service.

<strong>/run/</strong><em>name</em><strong>.pid</strong>
: A running service's process id (<strong>/run</strong> is in memory, mounted by <strong>/etc/rc</strong>).

## Examples

```text
rc mcsshd enable
rc mcsshd start
rc mcsshd status
```

## Notes

Linux has several: sysvinit's scripts in <strong>/etc/init.d</strong> are shell scripts that take start and stop themselves; OpenRC's set settings and may define their own functions (as these do, with OpenRC's names, in Lua: mcos's scripting language); systemd has units. <strong>rc.conf</strong>'s <em>name\_enable</em> is FreeBSD's, as is <strong>/etc/rc.d</strong>. Services start in <strong>rc.conf</strong>'s order, with no dependencies between them.

## See also

<strong>sh</strong>(1), <strong>kill</strong>(1), <strong>ps</strong>(1)
